feedback: If the child says 'resistance means broken/off', show a dim-but-lit bulb: every component has some resistance; it limits the current rather than stopping it.
If 'current' and 'voltage' are swapped while describing the brightening, restate: 'adding a cell in series, the same way round, adds VOLTAGE — the push — which drives a larger CURRENT — the flow.'
When the loop is switched to branches, confirm the child first describes the path, then names it 'parallel' — noting KS2 investigates series only, so parallel here is only the contrast term.
activities.intendedInsight: The relational words (current, voltage, resistance, series vs parallel) name behaviours, not just definitions — seeing 'more voltage → brighter' and 'series vs parallel → different path' maps each word onto something observable.
learnerActions: Work with a small circuit where dynamic words change what happens: add a cell in series, facing the same way as the others (more voltage), and watch the bulb brighten, using a bulb rated for the extra voltage; name the change using the word 'voltage'.

Reconfigure the loop between a single loop (series) and branches (parallel) and describe, using the words, what is different about the PATH — treating parallel as the named contrast, not a circuit to investigate at KS2.
Say how 'resistance' shows itself: adding a component with more resistance into the single loop (in series) makes the bulb dimmer; resistance limits the current, it does not break the circuit.
activities.title: Make the words do their job (words that enact)

feedback: If current and voltage are swapped, use a sentence frame: 'the cell's VOLTAGE pushes a CURRENT that FLOWS' — voltage is the push, current is the flow.

If every circuit is called 'series' or any two-bulb circuit 'parallel', have the child describe the path FIRST, then name it: series = one single loop; parallel = branches. A single loop with two bulbs is still series.
If 'component' is used for nothing in particular, ask the child to point to the component and state its job.
For the design task, check the described circuit forms a complete loop and that each named word matches its actual role in the design.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct USE places each term in its right role in the sentence; a child who has only memorised definitions can recite them yet still swap current for voltage or call any multi-bulb circuit 'parallel'. Threading the words through an accurate live description and through a circuit the child designs is the real evidence of understanding.
learnerActions: Given a working torch or series circuit, describe out loud how it works using current, voltage, resistance, series and component, saying what each word is DOING, not its dictionary meaning.

Aim for a description that places each term in its correct role, e.g. 'the cell provides the voltage that pushes a current around the series circuit; the current flows through each component — bulb, switch, wire; the bulb has resistance, which is why it glows and limits the current.'
Design a simple series circuit to meet a stated goal (e.g. a circuit with a switch that turns a buzzer on and off), sketch it, and describe your design using the correct vocabulary.
Then adjust the description for a new configuration: what would change in your words if the bulbs were in parallel (branches) instead of one single loop (series)?

Answer probing questions: 'You said the current flows — what is the voltage doing, is it also flowing or something different?' and 'This circuit has two bulbs in one single loop — is it series or parallel, and how do the words tell you?'
activities.title: Describe and design a working circuit, in role

feedback: For a conductor/insulator mis-sort, return to the lets-through vs blocks contrast using a real material.
For a series/parallel mis-sort, have the child trace whether there is one single loop or branches before choosing.

Treat these matching and sorting tasks as consolidation and checking; they can check classification but do not by themselves require the child to construct an original spoken or written description or to handle real components.
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting and completing descriptions consolidates the vocabulary and checks that boundaries between confusable terms hold, especially conductor/insulator and series/parallel.
learnerActions: Match each word to its component or meaning (e.g. switch ↔ opens/closes the loop; insulator ↔ blocks electricity).
Sort materials or components into conductor vs insulator, and sort circuit features into series vs parallel.
Complete fill-the-gap circuit descriptions such as 'the ___ pushes the ___ round the loop' using the correct terms.
activities.title: Sort, match and complete circuit descriptions
